title: The Trial in Lisbon
teaser: One message could change Omar’s life.
paragraphs: Omar is nineteen. He lives in Tanta with his mother and his little sister, Mariam. Every evening after work, he plays football on a dusty pitch near the train station.
One night, his phone buzzes. It is a message from a man called Mr. Tavares. “I saw your video online,” he writes. “I am a coach in Lisbon. Can you come for a trial next month?”

Omar reads the message ten times. He is excited, but he is also nervous. The ticket is expensive, and he has never left Egypt. He shows the message to his mother. She is quiet for a long time. Then she smiles. “We will find the money,” she says. “You must go.”

For four weeks, Omar trains harder than ever. He runs at six in the morning before work. He practises his left foot until it hurts. His friends help him too. They collect a little money every week for his ticket.

On the day of the trial, the pitch in Lisbon is green and perfect. Omar’s legs feel heavy. Then he remembers the dusty pitch in Tanta, and his friends, and his mother’s smile. He takes a deep breath, gets the ball, and runs.

title: How a Football Transfer Really Works
teaser: Why does a player cost 50 million? Here is what happens behind the scenes.
paragraphs: Every summer, fans refresh their phones waiting for transfer news. But what actually happens when a club buys a player? It is more complicated than paying money and taking a photo with a shirt.

First, a club needs a reason. Maybe their best defender is getting old, or they want a faster winger. Scouts watch many players, often for months, and send reports about their skills, their fitness and even their attitude in training.

When the club chooses a player, it contacts the player’s current club. This is where the negotiation starts. The selling club wants the highest price, and the buying club wants the lowest. They talk about a fixed fee, and sometimes extra payments, for example if the player scores a certain number of goals.

At the same time, the buying club must agree a contract with the player. This includes his salary, how many years he will stay, and other details. Most players have an agent who negotiates for them and takes a percentage.
Before anything is signed, the player has a medical. Doctors check his heart, his muscles and old injuries. A bad medical result can cancel the whole deal, even at the last minute.

Finally, the papers must reach the league before the transfer window closes. Clubs can only register new players during these windows, usually in summer and in January. That is why the last day, called deadline day, is often so dramatic.

title: Nour’s First Fight
teaser: The gym was her secret. Tonight, everyone will know.
paragraphs: Nour is twenty-two and studies law in Alexandria. Two years ago, she walked past a small boxing gym near her university. She was curious, so she went inside. The coach, Captain Hamdy, gave her old gloves and said, “Come back tomorrow.” She did.

Now Nour trains five days a week. She skips rope, hits the heavy bag and runs on the Corniche at sunrise. Her body is stronger, but the biggest change is in her mind. She is calmer and more confident.

Tonight is her first real fight. It is only an amateur competition, but her hands are shaking. Her family is in the crowd. Her father did not like the idea at first, but now he is wearing a T-shirt with her name on it.
The bell rings. Her opponent is tall and fast. In the first round, Nour gets hit twice and feels dizzy. In the corner, Captain Hamdy speaks slowly. “Breathe. Keep your hands up. Move your feet.”

In the second round, Nour remembers every morning on the Corniche. She moves, she waits, and she lands a clean punch. When the fight ends, the judges choose her opponent. Nour loses, but she is smiling. Her father is shouting her name.

title: Why Fighters Step on a Scale
teaser: Weight classes, weigh-ins and the dangerous habit of cutting weight.
paragraphs: In boxing, MMA and wrestling, fighters are divided into weight classes, such as lightweight or heavyweight. The idea is simple: a heavier person usually hits harder and is harder to move, so fights are fairer when both people are a similar size.

To make sure everyone follows the rules, there is a weigh-in, usually the day before the fight. Each fighter stands on a scale in front of officials and cameras. If someone is too heavy, they may have to pay part of their money to the opponent, or the fight may be cancelled.

Here is the strange part. Many fighters do not normally live at their fight weight. In the weeks before a fight, they diet. Then, in the last few days, many of them lose water on purpose: they drink less, sit in saunas and sweat in heavy clothes. This is called cutting weight.

After the weigh-in, they drink and eat again, and by fight night they can be several kilos heavier. Some fighters believe this gives them an advantage, because they are bigger than the official limit.

However, doctors warn that extreme weight cutting is dangerous. A body without enough water is weaker, the brain is less protected, and in rare cases fighters have been seriously hurt. Because of this, some organisations now check fighters’ water levels or hold weigh-ins on the same day as the fight.

title: Ninety Days
teaser: Karim wanted big muscles in one month. The gym had other plans.
paragraphs: Karim is eighteen. In January, he joined a gym near his house in Nasr City. On the first day, he lifted the heaviest weights he could find. The next morning, he could not lift his arms to brush his teeth.
An older man at the gym, Uncle Sayed, laughed when he saw him. Uncle Sayed is sixty and very fit. “Slow down,” he said. “Muscles grow when you rest, not only when you lift.”

Uncle Sayed gave Karim a simple plan. Three days a week, full-body exercises. Good form first, then heavier weights. Sleep for eight hours. Eat eggs, beans, chicken and lots of vegetables. And write everything in a notebook.

For the first month, Karim did not see a big difference in the mirror. He wanted to quit. But his notebook showed something else: every week he lifted a little more, and he could run for longer without stopping.
After ninety days, Karim took a photo and put it next to his first photo. The change was clear. But he was proudest of the notebook. It was full of small wins, one page at a time.

title: What Protein Actually Does
teaser: Do you need shakes to build muscle? Probably not.
paragraphs: Walk into any gym and you will hear people talking about protein. Some carry big shakers everywhere. But what is protein, and how much do you really need?

Protein is one of the three main parts of food, together with carbohydrates and fat. Your body breaks it down into small pieces called amino acids and uses them to repair and build tissues, including muscles, skin and hair.

When you train hard, you create tiny damage in your muscle fibres. During rest, your body uses amino acids to repair them and make them a little stronger. That is why protein matters, but also why sleep and rest days matter just as much.

Most sports scientists recommend about 1.6 grams of protein per kilo of body weight per day for people who want to build muscle. For a 70-kilo person, that is around 110 grams. It sounds like a lot, but eggs, foul, lentils, chicken, fish, milk and yoghurt can provide most of it.

So are protein shakes necessary? Not really. They are simply a convenient way to get protein when you are busy. They are not magic, and eating more protein than your body can use will not build extra muscle. Training consistently, eating enough and sleeping well are what make the difference.

title: Grandpa’s Old Fiat
teaser: It hasn’t moved for fifteen years. Youssef wants to drive it.
paragraphs: In the garage under Youssef’s building in Giza, there is an old white Fiat 128. It belonged to his grandfather. Nobody has driven it for fifteen years. It is covered in dust, and one tyre is flat.

Youssef is twenty and loves cars. He watches repair videos every night. One day, he asks his father, “Can I try to fix Grandpa’s car?” His father laughs. “That car is dead,” he says. “But you can try.”

Youssef starts with the easy things. He cleans the car, changes the flat tyre and buys a new battery. Then he takes the engine apart slowly and puts every small piece in a labelled bag. A mechanic on his street, Am Reda, helps him when he gets stuck.
It takes three months and all his savings. Some nights, nothing works and he wants to give up. But Am Reda always says, “Old engines are simple. They just need patience.”

Finally, one Friday morning, Youssef turns the key. The engine coughs, coughs again, and then starts. The whole street comes to watch. His father is silent for a moment. Then he gets into the passenger seat and says, “Take me to the Nile.”

title: How an Electric Car Moves Without Petrol
teaser: No gears, no oil changes, no engine noise. So what is under the bonnet?
paragraphs: A normal car burns petrol inside its engine. Small explosions push pistons up and down, and this movement finally turns the wheels. An electric car does the same job in a completely different way.

Instead of a fuel tank, it has a large battery, usually under the floor. The battery stores electricity, and an electric motor uses that electricity to create a magnetic field that spins the motor. The motor turns the wheels directly, so most electric cars do not need a gearbox with many gears.

This simple design has some interesting effects. Electric cars are very quiet, and they accelerate quickly from a stop, because the motor gives its full power immediately. They also have fewer moving parts, which means less maintenance: no oil changes and fewer things to break.
Electric cars can also recover energy. When the driver slows down, the motor works in reverse like a generator and sends a little electricity back to the battery. This is called regenerative braking.

The biggest challenges are range and charging. A typical car can drive between 300 and 500 kilometres on one charge, and charging can take from twenty minutes at a fast charger to many hours at home. As batteries improve and more chargers are built, these problems are becoming smaller.

title: The Last Level
teaser: Ziad made a game in his bedroom. Now strangers are playing it.
paragraphs: Ziad is seventeen and loves video games. But he does not only play them. For one year, he has been making his own game on his old laptop. It is called Sand Runner. A small camel runs through the desert and jumps over snakes and cactus plants.

He learned everything from free videos online. When something did not work, he asked questions in forums. Sometimes he waited days for an answer. His little brother, Adam, was his first tester. Adam was honest. “Level three is boring,” he said. Ziad changed it.
In the summer, Ziad uploaded Sand Runner to a free games website. On the first day, five people played it. Three of them were his cousins. He felt disappointed.

But a week later, a small YouTuber in Brazil played it in a video. Suddenly, two thousand people downloaded it. Players left comments in English, Spanish and Arabic. Some found bugs. One player wrote, “The last level is too hard. I love it.”
Ziad read every comment. Then he opened his laptop and started a new file. He called it Sand Runner 2.

title: Why One More Game Is So Hard to Refuse
teaser: Game designers know exactly how your brain works.
paragraphs: It is 1 a.m. You promised yourself one more match, and now it is 3 a.m. This is not only a lack of self-control. Many games are carefully designed to keep you playing.

One tool is the reward loop. You complete a task, you get a reward, and the game immediately shows you the next task. Each reward releases a little dopamine, a chemical in the brain connected to motivation. Your brain learns that the next reward is just a few minutes away.

Another tool is unpredictable rewards. If you knew exactly what every loot box or chest contained, it would be less exciting. Because the result is random, your brain stays curious and wants to try again. Slot machines in casinos use the same idea, which is why some countries now limit loot boxes.

Games also use progress bars, daily challenges and streaks. These make you feel that stopping means losing something you have already built. Social features add pressure too: your team needs you, and your friends can see when you are online.

None of this means games are bad. The same techniques can make learning fun, and many games are creative and social. The key is to notice these tricks, so that you decide when to stop, and not the game.
